p: Sorry. I had to get some water in. I want to now touch a little bit on the closure of the migrant shelter and mail processing center. The Office of Asylum-seeker Operation was created in March 2023, and you know that that was a response to the influx of migrants in New York City. Can you provide an update on MOIA’s current involvement with the asylum-seeker response and how the city’s response and support has changed in this past year?

So, MOIA has always served all immigrants, both recnet arrivals and long-term residents regardless of which office or agency is established– you know, is running that given program. We continue to work with DSS and DHS to share timely updates and are providing front-facing material for their clients.
So, the– OASO’s responsibility was shifted to MOIA and

I can jump in here. I would say that as the Commissioner laid out, MOIA has always been central, and this is sort of a central theme of today’s hearing in regards to many responses that impact immigrants. I would say that when OASO was closing, we worked collaboratively with them to ensure that there were access points for subset populations for legal services. So, the example that I spoke about a little bit before in regards to young people who were identified as potentially such eligible is a group of individuals that we worked with to ensure that services continue to provided. As OASO was closing down or the asylum application help center in particular, because that’s where we had more of a role, we ensured that folks who were being served by them had access going to legal services.

Now, the last remaining shelter for migrants is planned to close by the end of 2026. This will result in roughly 2,000+ people being dispersed throughout the DHS system. How is the administration ensuring that the

immigrants affected by shelter closures receive timely and clear information in their preferred language about their options?
So, we’ve been working with DSS and DHS on language access, in particular, issues at Brookner [sp?] and continue to work with them as the need changes.

And we also learned that the administration is closing the centralized mail center for asylum-seekers which is located in the migrant shelter in the south Bronx, which is in my district. The mail center is scheduled to close at the end of this month in March. Do you know if the admin has a solution on how people will continue to receive important immigration court documents? As you know, this is very important, especially those who have used that addressed and are waiting for mail.

So, as individuals are re-integrated into DHS, they will receive mail at their assigned sites. We also understand through DHS that have been communicating with impacted individuals about mail forwarding. On sort of the

exact details, we would defer to DHS for the most current information.

Okay. This is why we need one agency so that we can get these answers. So, we’re going to switch gears a little bit and talk about advancing immigrant worker protections. I know that we’ll be talking about this a lot next month as well. But you know, obviously, many of our immigrant workers face exploitation and unsafe working conditions, and that is very often compounded by fear related to their immigration status. Last year, the State Department of Labor created the New York State Bank on online resources designed to connect job seekers with employment opportunities. So, my question here is how are immigrants informed about their rights at work? How is this disseminated? Are there costs associated with these measures?
Sorry. This is response– in regards to the New York State Bank?
I read ahead. Excuse me.
It’s alright.

I’m going to get back. Just put that question in your pocket. The question around the State Bank was MOIA’s usage of the New York State Bank, if any, and if sharing it as a resource– and has it shared it as a resource to any of the members of the community?
I think on that question, we’re going to have to circle back.

Got you. Alright, so now I’m going to my second one which you’ve heard. How are immigrants informed about their rights at work, and how is that information disseminated? And are there any costs, more importantly, with those languages other than English?

Yeah. So, MOIA’s working really closely with Deputy Mayor Sue [sp?] and her team to really further integrate MOIA into the economic justice portfolio which we’re very excited about. We’re looking to– you know, exploring opportunities and looking to expand collaboration with some of the other agencies in that same vertical, including DCWP, SBS and DOB. You know, one of my priorities, as I mentioned earlier a few times, is really to bolster the work of our outreach team

and we really look forward to sort of,you know, work with our partners at the Office of Mass Engagement and other agencies to really best determine like how do we conduct outreach to this particular population?

Yeah, I think we’ll learn, you know, especially next month about like the impact that that has on our small businesses on our business communities, our commercial corridors and what we’re really seeing out on the streets. I’m going to take a pause to recognize Council Member Krishnan. Do you have a question? No? Not right now? Alright, he’s thinking on it. So, how does MOIA budge prioritize workforce development programs for immigrant communities?

So, currently MOIA’s program focuses on immigration legal services, Know Your Rights, English classes and other support services. In this– under this sort of new administration and new MOIA, I think being part of that economic justice portfolio is something that we’re currently still assessing and figuring out ways to actually integrate that throughout the office and through the existing programs. And with respect to your specific question on your funding, no specific

funding was allocated to MOIA for this particular purpose, but we are continuing to assess our programming and initiative needs to identify some of these gaps.

Okay, so there may be funding requests in the future for this if you see that this is something that is necessary. So, for English language learning and support centers, how successful has that program been in terms of attracting new participants? And what criteria is being used to measure that success?

So, on English language learners, I want to make sure we have the right numbers for you. We had in FY26 so far 2,083 unique learners and about 750 graduates. We are– through this program we’ve delivered 73 classes across three of the library systems reaching about 1,700 unique learners and 576 graduates, and then the in-house We Speak program that MOIA runs has also delivered 23 classes across Queens, Manhattan, the Bronx, and Brooklyn to reach 382 unique learners and 174 graduates.

And so, the outcome and the impacts, they’re being tracked by

graduates, right? Is there any other– are there any other measures in that program that you track to signal success?

Yeah. So, per quarter, we are keeping track of unique learner numbers, but we are also keeping track of regularity of attendance, certificate eligibility, all of that is really tracked to assess the neighborhood or the branch that, you know, what their needs are and the applicability of services. In addition to attendance numbers, facilitator observations, curriculum packets also include a survey, and so we get a multilingual learner survey where individuals can self report on demographic information like, you know, origin, the borough of residence, you know, time learning English, and any other feedback that they have. So, the survey is another way for us to capture that information.

And is that– does that survey– because obviously there’s less than half that have graduated that have come in. So, does it speak to some of the barriers that they may find going to the program, attending it and completing it?

Yeah. So, to what the Commissioner laid out I think there’s really three key components of the work and how we track. It’s the unique learners, and the attendance and the graduate, because– and also sort of understanding how this program might be different from your– you know, more traditional adult literacy class is that this is really the first time that learners might be open to even speaking another language, and an entry point to further services. So, a key for us is also ensuring that folks are showing up and that attendance is one of the key factors that we look at as well.
So, how do you track demand for the services? How do you identify a community or where this service should be provided?
We’re currently not tracking that, because we– the program as we know it, it’s sort of new, at least one or two years, but we’re certainly open to assessing that.
Do you know which organizations are contracted out for this program?

There are three library branches, New York Public Library,

Brooklyn Public Library, and the Queens Public Library.
And was there an RFP process to receive the funding for that program that they have to go through that at the libraries or were they just designated?
No RFP process.
Okay, and in total what was anticipated to be allocated in fiscal 2027?
So, it’s $500,000 per library system. $200,000 is what we started out with and then $300,000 was added additional to that program. I don’t know if you want to talk about the breakdown.

Yeah. So, this is for FY26. For FY27, as I mentioned earlier, we did get an additional $1.5 million that has been baselined for this program. So, for FY27 we are looking at about $2.1 million baselined for English learning and support centers. We are still in the process of figuring out how all of that funding will be allocated. And just very briefly to go back to

your question about the RFP, we– the libraries were designated this funding when we first launched this program because we had already had a partnership with them to provide programming. This has allowed us to have– to meet the demand for the asylum-seeker community that was asking for all of these classes to be readily available for them throughout the city. So, it did allow us as, you know, as an office to meet that demand. Again, now that we have baseline funding we are going to be evaluating all of our programs and then making an assessment, you know, short term and long term in terms of allocations.

Yeah, I hope so, because you know, I love my libraries and I think that they’re a great place to house this especially when you're trying to turn it over really quickly with the organization that you trust, that you can provide the services, but I know services like this are needed in so many different pockets of communities. It’s very difficult to move around the city as a newcomer to the city and get access to resources, and so I really do hope the RFP speaks to that and that we can track where that need is and identify that so we can properly provide that

service. It’s important. And so before I move into the next topic which will be around some of our legal support centers and Action NYC, I’m going to allow our amazing– Council Member Joseph has another question for you, a quick commercial break as we called it.
No, it actually– it’s along the lines that you were asking.
Perfect.

Right? I know about We Speak, because I taught that program. Is there a possibility where there could be a partnership with District 79 that’s already doing that work? I think that should be a conversation when we talk about interagencies. D79 does the ESL, the GED, but it serves a large immigrant community which is already embedded in the New York City Public School system.
Council Member, that’s a great idea and something that we will definitely explore.
See, told you, Chair.
I love this. We’re going to be ping-ponging all day. This is great.
Thank you so much.

That was really good. No, of course. So, for the immigration legal support centers, we know that the Preliminary Plan includes $11.6 million in baseline funding for legal support centers. The former Commissioner changed the program’s name from Action NYC to MOIA’s Immigration Legal Support Centers. Can you explain the changes in the new model, and how have they improved services?

So, I’ll start and I’ll kick it over to my colleague, as I’m also learning the sort of shift and change. Some of the changes, as I understand it, include adjusting really the number of contracted providers, funding levels, deliverables, target population, and the geographic reach, and so that is included– it’s not just the name change. I think there was also a more holistic deliberate approach to this. I think at the heart of the redesign was the goal of embedding legal service providers within immigrant-dense neighborhoods

alongside organizations that are equipped to really deliver immigration services in a culturally and linguistically-informed way. And so, you know, the question of, you know, whether this has– you know, what the shift was. You know, I think the shift, you know, into communities that can service and have longstanding sort of relationships is where you saw a large sort of shift in the actual programming.
And how many centers are currently open?

We have 29 unique providers across 38 contracts. So, there are 25 Legal Support Centers that are working with a three-year contract, and then there’s an additional 13 that were sort of former Action NYC partners who were also given an opportunity to apply for funding in FY26.
So, will there be additional centers that possibly open under this program?

I think that’s part of the assessment that we’re working on, and figuring out what has been working and what hasn’t. And if you would allow me, because I think

the numbers speak for themselves. But you know, the program, we still haven’t hit our first birthday yet. So we’re getting there, and we’re working to closely assess the needs and if the model is working or not, but I just wanted to give you the number, because to-date there has been significant across the new support centers. The program has recorded 8,756 screenings, and 3,727 filings through the first half of FY26 and into quarter three. If you compare this to 7,656 screenings and 4,684 filings that were done for all of FY2025. So, just to say that the providers have been going above and beyond and working, and also the demand of course to acknowledge the increase, but I just wanted to share that with you, because we found that number to be an important indicator. Of course, there’s other assessments and things to that extent, but I wanted to share that number with you.
No, I appreciate that number. Can you talk about some of the other assessments? I know that there’s a lot of assessing going on at this time. So,--
[interposing] [inaudible].
What are some of those things that you’re looking at?

Yeah. I mean, we have direct communications with our providers and we are about to start and roll out our quarter three convos [sic] with them. Parts of the conversations are whether or not, you know, we’re on track to meet deliverables, but also if there are additional services that they want to provide, additional needs that they’re seeing on the ground, things like that as we’re sort of doing this massive look under the hood with all our programs at

And kicking the tires, too, I’m assuming, right? So, the Council has provided MOIA with $850,000 to cover fees for applications and other operational expenses for MOIA-funded legal providers. Can you provide us a status on how that funding is being used?

So, that particular funding was allocated across 27 providers. 24 of them have this funding already reflected in their FY26 budgets and providers are– did they put you on the clock? Oh, my goodness. Providers are also submitting updated budgets to be able to invoice and

to pass for. There are three providers out of the 27 that have contract amendments that are in progress with our contracting agency, DSS, to add to this funding. I don’t know if there’s anything more, Jas, that you wanted to add to that.

Well, very quickly, in total actually that– the total amount that went over to those filing fees was about $1 million. We use the $850,000 as well as about $172 million that was left over from the $4.4 million that was provided by the Council for legal services. So, we make sure that we utilize that funding to be able to provide this much needed support to more providers.

Okay, great. And so for the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative, the Preliminary Plan includes $2.2 million in fiscal 26 for the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative program. I know we’ve spoken a lot about this, but are there specific immigrant populations that are facing more challenges than others that were reported by the collaborative, and if so, how are you supporting them and prioritizing?

So, we touched a little bit on this earlier with folks who have lost TPS, but there are several populations that are facing a number of challenges including those who have lost TPS or whose status is really in limbo. Those are the key populations that we are currently focused on. There are undocumented individuals more broadly are facing increased fear and uncertainty because of the intensified federal enforcement. So that we know, as Chair you’ve mentioned, has had a chilling effect on their willingness to access city services. So we’re focused on undocumented individuals as well. And then we’re also seeing a significant need as we talk to our contracted providers amongst unaccompanied minors and mixed-status families who are navigating this federal– very hostile federal landscape.
So, in terms of the Immigration Legal Support Hotline, the budget also allocated for legal support it includes $632,000 roughly in fiscal 2026. How many people currently staff the hotline?

So, the hotline employs seven full-time counselors. The counselors at

the hotline speak English, French, Haitian-Creole, Spanish, Urdu.
And what are the hours of operation? You said it was–

So, they’ve been expanded beyond our typical Monday through Friday, nine to five. So the expanded hours right now Monday and Wednesday from 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., Tuesday, Thursday, Friday from 9:00 to 6:00. The last Saturday of the month has been added and is– the hotline is available from 9:00 to 5:00.
So, as we know, you know, part of the defense here with imminent deportation is that people may need to get to somebody really quickly. So, what should someone do outside of those operating hours?

I think directly with providers, they should be engaging with them. I mean, we’re currently providing, you know, materials and listing that is available to both the providers and connecting individuals both about NYFUP and the RLC, and that information is in fact available in top 10 languages. If a caller calls the hotline during operating hours, we know that they’re going to be

directed to staff, and if they call– I think there’s an option, if I’m correct– staff can correct me. There is an option for folks who call outside of operating hours to leave a message and have their call be returned.
Are they connected in any way outside of operating hours? Like, press one to be connected to?

Yeah, to add to what the Commissioner said, after hours they’re just asked to call back during the normal operating hours. But it’s an issue that we’re going to bring back, because I know there were flags about after-hour services. It’s something that we are looking into. When a caller dials in– I’m going to try to get it right– they are prompted to IVR system which asks them like what language they want to choose. Right now, we have Spanish, English, Haitian-Creole, and I think one more, and we’re working on rolling out additional languages by the end of the spring.

Yeah we have, I believe, 800 different languages that we speak in this city, and so we really are always going to push

for more language access and having that information on that.
If you would allow me, Chair?
Go ahead, yes, please.

Besides the hotline operators that we have that speaks the number of languages that the Commissioner laid out, operators also have access to Language Line which opens up the many additional languages that might be needed depending on who calls.
And you said there were seven now. How many were last– were there last year?
I can circle back with that number. I don’t have it handy.
Okay. So, how do you anticipate that the demand will change in the coming year, and can the level of funding that is put there adequately support those needs?

Well, we hope that individuals keep calling the hotline to receive services. That’s always a hope for us. In

regards to additional assessments for future funding needs, that’s part of the larger work that we’re currently doing across our programs.

Alrighty [sic]. We’re getting through a lot, so thank you all for getting through this with me. I know it seems like there’s a lot here, but ultimately what we’re trying to get to is that makes sure that you have all of the resources that you need to do this important work. We’re seeing it on the ground from our constituents, and we want to make sure that when we’re fighting for this budget that we make sure you have everything that you need covered, but I know that there has been– for example, for the asylum-seeker legal services that there was funding that was cut for ASLAN [sic] in fiscal 26 and for fiscal 26 only. The City Council restored it for $5 million. Can you explain a little bit about why that funding was cut?

So, I’ll start and my team can fill in some of the blanks. My understanding is that the funding for ASLAN and the navigation centers was actually consolidated into MOIA’s Legal Support Centers funding.
And to be more specific, that funding was repurposed to allow– to provide the one-year extension to the former Action NYC providers that currently have a one-year contract with us for FY26.
So, that’s part of the $7.6 million for fiscal 2026?

Correct. So, in order for us to be able to continue this one-year contract for those 13 providers in FY26, we utilize the– we repurpose the ASLAN and also navigation center’s funding as well as the $4.4 million allocated by the Council. That has allowed us to provide those one-year contracts for this fiscal year.

Okay, alright. This is what I mean about having to shift and move, and move there. So, I want to get into Local Law 73. You know, as you know, it was meant to develop a survey of newly-arrived immigrants, especially those who have arrived recently. Can you provide an update on the survey development and the administration? Just on the survey development first, and then we’ll get to the rest.

Yeah, Chair, and I think it’s like– it was a pairing between 73 and 74 if I’m not mistaken. Currently, the DOHMH is in charge of administering said survey. MOIA has supported them, has consulted with them, but DOHMH would have sort of the latest on where things are.
And are we able to obtain the surveys to know what kind of questions were included in those surveys?
We’re happy to circle back just because we’re not the authors of them, but we can check with our colleagues.
Okay. And do you know how many asylum-seekers or migrants were involved in each survey?
We don’t have that number now because the survey is actively being done. So we wouldn't have access to that data right now.
Okay. And has there been any issues with carrying out that law, creating that survey? Any barriers that you've seen for that agency?

Again, like we’ll touch base with them, but I would say to you that I know that part of what we were also working on is that people were moving, things to that extent, but we can have a better, more concrete response to you once we touch base with our colleagues.

Okay, we’ll be circling back on that. And the Preliminary Plan also includes $16.9 million for the IOI Deportation Defense initiative. What is the projected budget for the IOI Deportation Initiative for fiscal year 27?
We are going to have to confirm that for you. That program is actually managed by DSS, so we don’t have oversight of that particular program.

Okay. So, I’ll hold for that, but just so that you know what I’m asking, it’s both for the projected budget for IOI Deportation Defense and also for the IOI Immigration Opportunity Initiative for fiscal– both for fiscal 27.
We’ll follow up.

Thank you. It was also announced that the Department of Small Business Services is creating a new Office of Vendor Services as required by City Council bill– sorry– that passed last year. The Office of Vendor Services will be tasked with supporting the city’s estimated 23,000 street vendors, nearly all of whom are immigrants. Is MOIA planning to work closely with this office as nearly all street vendors are immigrants?
We’re very excited to hear of this announcement, are very much looking forward to teaming up and working closely with the Department of Vendor Services.
Do you know if language capacity will be available for this office? Do you know?
I actually don’t. We can follow up.

Okay, because I know that the needs of delivery workers, street vendors, you know, they’re at the forefront of the Council’s agenda. As you know, we have some really strong champions in the council, and so we want to

understand– can you describe how you partner to support coalitions of delivery workers, street vendors, small businesses?

Yeah, I think part of what we’re also excited about is that we’re under this new portfolio with Deputy Mayor Su, and we’re looking forward to building more robust relationships across agencies, but also with organizations. I would say that we have been in touch with the deliveristas in the past, particularly when issues connected to legal issues came up, and we have been in touch with them. But as the Commissioner said, there’s more intentionality that we are hoping to move forward with especially with the new offices and the office that was created with– the Street Vendor Project in particular.

I am excited as well, as well as most of the champions and the City Council. We’ll be tracking this, and we’re looking forward to, you know, continuing this work and having you back to ask specific questions around small businesses and how we support them, as well as a number of other topics that we’ll be working, much like you, in collaboration with my council– my other

council team in terms of committees. So, there’ll be some of that happening in the near future. For now I want to thank you for your time and your testimony. We are going to be moving into the public comment section. We don’t have anyone else here. There’s no one online, Council Members. So, we will be taking a short break for those of you so I can move my feet around, and thank you so much, Commissioner. It’ll be about five to 10 minutes.
Chair, we want to thank you and your team as well.
Thank you. [break]
Quiet down. Can everyone get their seats? We’re about to begin.

Thank you so much for coming back. We are now going to ask our invited guests, former Speaker of the New York City Council, Melissa Mark-Viverito, to give testimony at today’s hearing. That’s right. Alright, don’t– let’s do the thing. Let’s do the thing. When you’re ready, just press the button and go.

Okay. Alright, well good afternoon. Buenos tardes to everybody. It

really is wild to be here. I’ve not been in this building since I left office, and it’s wonderful to see the upgrades and everything. And to everybody that’s in this room, all the advocates that do the work each and every day on behalf of our immigrant communities, I commend you all for the work and for being here. It was a pleasure when I was in office to be able to work side by side with many of you. So, good afternoon to the Chairwoman of this committee who happens to be my Councilwoman, Elsie Encarnacion. You know, we all know that– the dark times that we are living in. There's a national siege on immigrant families and the communities we’re a part of, and it’s upon us. This moment demands more from us. New York and other cities must stand strong for the human rights and values at the core of our local policies. This city does not buckle under pressure. We act. Our upcoming budget negotiations are a critical opportunity to aggressively meet these dangerous times, including by bolstering offices and services on the front lines of work and leadership. ICE and Border Patrol agents masked and dressed in full combat gear have flooded cities across the country and now our airports. These agents have become the

foot soldiers of a cruel, authoritarian regime, unleashing indiscriminate violence against anyone they perceive as other, citizen and non-citizen alike. Sadly, it is crystal clear to agents that they will not be held accountable for their actions, even in the most egregious of cases. In fact, the White House routinely posts memes and AI-generated videos that celebrate ICE and Border Patrol’s cruelty and advance not so thinly-veiled white supremacist propaganda. There’s no denying that a year and a half into Trump’s second term, his administration is unapologetic and scapegoating non-white people, flouting due process, increasing surveillance, all while lining the pockets of the president’s cronies in the most corrupt administration ever. New York City has grown, become stronger over time and thrives thanks to the contributions of immigrants, and its rich diversity attracts millions of visitors and dollars to the city each year, providing more to our local economy than what they receive in any type of services, despite what ignorant critics may spew. In recognition of this sanctuary, protections have been embedded into the fabric of our city. Since the 1980s both Republican and Democratic mayors have recognized

that communities are safer when immigrants do not fear reporting crime to the police. Similarly, communities are healthier when all who reside within it can access health care and financially sound when there are diverse job opportunities and strong worker protections. With over 3 million immigrants calling New York City home and many more living in mixed-status households, the city must ensure immigrants feel safe accessing city services. The Council has an exemplary record of taking strong legislative action to protect their rights and ensure that city agencies and law enforcement can focus on their prior duty, ensuring the safety and wellbeing of our city. To that end, the Council under the leadership of this previous Council Speaker passed legislation that prohibits local law enforcement from entering into 287G agreements which would allow them to cooperate with ICE on civil immigration enforcement. Additional laws ensure that city resources and time are not used in support of federal immigration enforcement, including by prohibiting ICE access to Rikers Island. We also passed detainer laws that protect the immigrants due process rights, by ensuring that the NYPD, Department of Correction,

and Department of Probation only honor detainer requests when they are accompanied by judicial warrant, and we set a national standard by investing millions to fund legal and other services that provided critical safety net, one which only has expanded since then thanks to the leadership of our New York City Council. As our federal elected representatives attempt to reign in ICE and Border Patrol’s most egregious behavior through funding negotiations and cities around the country passed laws similar to those we’ve had on the books for years, New York City must continue to be a national leader in partnership with New York State. At the state level, I want to commend Senator Gounardes and Assemblywoman Reyes, prime sponsors of the New York for All Act, and hope to see this legislation passed as part of the current state budget negotiations. This will permanently bring New York State more in line with our city sanctuary laws and offer critical protections to millions of New Yorkers. Here in NYC, our wonderful New York City, with a City Council that is new and mayor at the helm, we must continue to fight federal overreach and hate while advancing policies and initiatives that enhance our

longstanding efforts to promote the inclusion, protection, and celebration of immigrant New Yorkers. But today, many of the programs intended to support immigrant New Yorkers exist across multiple agencies, creating a patchwork system that can be difficult to track, coordinate and strengthen. This fragmentation makes it harder to ensure accountability, maintain a cohesive strategy and quickly respond to the evolving needs of our communities. So to meet this moment with the urgency it demands, something that many advocates have been advocating for over the years, we should really take the next setp and consider establishing a standalone immigration agency, one that can bring together the various contracts, initiatives that are currently spread across these agencies, ensuring that work is coordinated, nimble, strategic, and fully aligned with the values we have long upheld. So at a time when immigrant communities are being targeted and tested at every level, our response must be equally intentional. Obviously, as part of that demand is also the fact that all the services that are currently financed and funded should not see a dollar withheld. If anything, an understanding we have difficult times, we should see

an expansion of possible– of some of those critical services. I’m sure many of which you’ll hear from the advocates today, but I think that having this comprehensive and city agency, and the weight that that comes and brings with it is really imperative, again, so that the agency could be nimble and deal with what is to come. We know that New York City is going to be on the front lines of that. So, we– at a time when immigrant communities are being targeted and tested at every level, our response must be equally intentional. We have led before and we must continue to lead now not only by defending our policies, but by strengthening the systems that make them real in people’s lives. So, gracias [speaking Spanish]. Thank you for inviting me here today, and I appreciate the opportunity.

Thank you. And thank you for coming, obviously. Yes, we got to– obviously, you know, for those of you who don’t know, I served under Council Member– when she was Council Member, not as Speaker, for six years. And so you do this work day in and day out from the day you stepped into office to the day I left your office. I’m proud to be here as one of your– one of the people that

you’ve really grown into this space, and I hope that I make you proud in the work that I do here today, and that I carry on. So, all of you will be witness that is, you know, mentorship. This is what happens when you really do the work, not just, you know, for the whole city, but you really look at your community and you look at people that can really take on the work and champion it moving forward, because the work never stops, and we need good people at the forefront. So, thank you so much for that, and [inaudible]

[interposing] The last– I just want to say to the people in this room it is the work that you do that has– gives us the ability to be successful in the work that we accomplish, right? The detainer laws that we talk about that we have in the City of New York, the getting ICE out of Rikers, that only came out of the advocacy that some of the groups when they met with me said this is happening in our city, we need to respond. So, please, I know the times are tough and things get difficult, but the work that you do does make a difference and it impacts people’s lives. So thank you for that.

Thank you. I will now open the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. Thank you, Chairperson Encarnacion and the honorable members of the Immigration Committee, and the Council finance team. I can’t live without. My name is Monique Francis, the newly appointed Executive Director at CUNY Citizenship Now. I’m here on behalf of the dedicated team of 58 City Council-funded staff and more than 400 active volunteers. In this time of escalating need, Citizenship Now has remained steadfast in our commitment to serving immigrant New Yorkers. Since starting in 2010, funding from the City Council has supported more than 80,000 individuals all on the path to citizenship. This includes in district one-and-one consultations, monthly community application assistance events, and most recently our virtual consultation series. For these New Yorkers, our services are free and are a vital lifeline. This helps them to remain in the United States while building a more stable future in the city they call home. This fiscal year alone our organization received more than 30,000 calls. In response we prioritize general inquiries to attorneys through our contact center hotline. More than 3,000 of those calls resulted in consultations and completed

applications. We respectfully urge the council to sustain its support for programs in the FY2027 fiscal year budget. We request the renewal of the $4.6 million allocation and for our ASLAN supplemental asylum services, we request continued funding of $845,951. CUNY Citizenship Now is making measurable difference in empowering immigrant New Yorkers. On May 16th we will hold our signature spring citizenship drive at John Jay College, a partnership with state and city agencies, nonprofit organization, and corporate law firms with a goal of helping 300 permanent residents complete their citizenship application. We ask that you show your support by showing up. Thank you for continued partnership. I welcome any questions.

Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, Chair Encarnacion. My name is Samira and I’m from Morocco. Firstly, I would like to say thank you. Thank you for giving me the chance to talk to you today, and I’m so glad to share my gratitude to City Tech Adult Learning Center and for the City Council Members. As once said, one teacher, one book, and one pencil can change the world which means that education is a power tool to change lives. As

many immigrants, including myself, the hardest part of starting a new life is the language. Language is truly a bridge to integration. As a mother, not being able to communicate made it hard for me to support my children in some things like reading, helping with homework, connecting with teachers, and getting more involved in school projects. I have experience that feeling when I know what to do, but I do not have the right words. Feeling frustrated and unable to help is what motivate me– motivates me to work on my language and improve it. Once I started learning English, everything began to change. I became more confident in communication by overcoming the language barrier and was able to support my children towards success. I’m glad today to say that City Tech Learning Center made this possible for me and for many immigrants who cannot afford English classes in private institutions. Without this program, immigrants might lose the chance to be included and connected to their communities. On behalf of all my classmates, I would like to say thank you City Tech Adult Learning Center for offering this program. Thank you City Hall for funding and support units. You are not just helping

with money, you are opening wide doors for immigrants to a brighter future. Thank you all for your attention.

Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Kalud [sp?], and today I want to share my experience learning English. I came to America in 2001 with my husband and my daughter from Syria. When I first arrived, I did not know how to speak English. Simple things like talking to others or asking for help felt very difficult. One of the biggest challenge for me was helping my daughter with her homework and speaking with her teachers. I wanted to support her, but I often felt upset, because I could not fully understand or express myself. Over the years, I had four more children. I learned very basic English by listening and trying my best in everyday situation, but I never really had the time to focus on my learning– the English correctly because I was busy raising my family. Now that my children are older, some in college and some in middle school, I finally felt more [inaudible] to learn English. I want to be more independent and understand everything around me. I was referred to this program by my friend Miriam [sp?] and decide to

sign up. I hope this will help me improve my English and enjoy it even more than I ever imagined. Through this program, I have learned so much. I have become more confident speaking with other without needing translation. I have also learned how to speak in public which is something I could not have imagined doing years ago. In this future, I hope to get my GED and become a medical assistant. I want to thank you for listening to us. We ask for your strong support for this program because it thoroughly deserves it. Thank you.

Good afternoon, member of this committee and ladies and gentlemen. My name is Ramon Epsinal and it is an honor and a privilege for me to be here at this Immigration Committee hearing, along with all those who like me have come with a single purpose to advocate for our education. My request today is to ask Councilwoman Crystal Hudson, representing District 35 which include my community of Fort Greene and surrounding area, and all her colleagues to advocate for better

education. We need more resources invest in all education programs at the school and university so that other like me can see their dream come true someday. And I personally, I believe that every New Yorker has the right to better education program. And I want to remind you guys that you didn’t elect us, we elected you to represent us. This is why I’m begging you to help us, to support us, right, in our education [inaudible] experience. Thank you very much. Thank you New York City, and God bless America.

Good afternoon everyone. My name is Ama Malak [sp?] and I’m one of many immigrants who has had the privilege of attending the ESL program at City Tech. I arrived in the United States one year ago from France. Today, I’m in my third semester, and I stand before to share with you why this program means so much to me. When I first come here, I felt lost. The language barrier was not just a challenge, it was isolating. I struggled to communicate, to express myself and to find my place. Then I joined the ESL program at City Tech and everything started to change. Step-by-step I gained confidence in speaking English and with that

confidence came new opportunities. Recently I started interviewing for jobs, something I could not have imagined when I first arrived. That is the true power of this program. It does not just teach English, it empowers people. It restores confidence. It opens doors and give us the ability to build a future and contribute to this country. For every dollar invested in this program, you are investing in someone’s future. Please continue to support and fund City Tech ESL programs because there are not just [inaudible] lives, they are building them. Thank you.

In the first, I want to thank City Hall for this opportunity, and I want to thank City Tech New York College of Technology [inaudible] for her support. When I come to United States I can’t speak or understand any word in English. Life, it was hard, but [inaudible] education help me to change my life. I learned English step-by-step, and I become more confident and independent. At that time, I start looking for something to practice my English. So I start working volunteer work with the City Tech

to translate– to help students and translate for them from Arabic [inaudible] to English to help register there. Later I start with my friends to create small platform like Zoom to make conversations [inaudible] to practice more. We start like three students and now it’s become more than 100. So, [inaudible] education made all this possible. That is why we [inaudible] ask you to support this program with funding so it can continue and welcome even more immigrants when need this opportunity. Thank you so much.

Good afternoon, Chair Encarnacion and members of the committee, and thank you for the opportunity to testify today and for the Council’s consideration of our renewal request for the New York Immigrant Family Unity Project, or NYIFUP. My name is Catherine Gonzalez. I am Associate General Counsel at Brooklyn Defender Services. Alongside the Bronx Defenders and Legal Aid Society, we serve as the city’s defender organizations providing free legal representation to detained immigrants through the NYIFUP program. For more than a decade, NYIFUP has been a national model for providing high-quality representation for immigrants in detained removal proceedings who cannot afford counsel. Thank you to City Council funding, New Yorkers facing deportation have had a lawyer by their side. While we have weathered enforcement surges before, what we are seeing now is without precedent. Since our last testimony in 2025, arrests have rapidly increased by ICE and new detention facilities have opened across the northeast and the

country. ICE is transferring New Yorkers within hours, often out of state, and sometimes thousands of miles away. We are currently representing New Yorkers detained in at least 15 states because they’ve been moved. For the people we serve, detention is existential loss of liberty, separation from family, and the very real risk of deportation to life-threatening conditions or countries where they have no ties or support. These enforcement tactics are designed to sever community ties and undermine due process. NYIFUP’s integration within public defender offices allows us to quickly act in an increasingly volatile system. NYIFUP is responding in real-time, conducting urgent interviews late at night or early in the morning, filing last-minute motions and preserving life-savings claims that might otherwise lost without a hearing. We’re also expanding litigation in federal courts to secure clients released through habeas petitions in-house and to vindicate their fundamental rights by pursuing critical appeals in the federal circuit courts. No New Yorker should face deportation alone, and we urge the Council to continue and deepen its commitment to NYIFUP in this new and brutal enforcement landscape.

Thank you for your continued commitment to protecting immigrant New Yorkers.

Hi, good afternoon, Chair Encarnacion, and members of the Committee. My name is Karla Ostolaza. I’m the Managing Director of the Immigration Practice at the Bronx Defenders. You’ve heard from my colleague the reality in which this work takes place right now. I want to focus on what your investment has made possible, despite the challenges. Your support has allowed us to grow, adopt, and meet community needs in ways that were simply not possible before. When the Trump administration began, our team must carry more than a a thousand pending cases for clients we had fought to free from detention, people now at risk of being detained again. Thanks to the Council’s increased funding, we expanded our capacity to take on an extraordinary influx of new clients while still providing excellent clients under representation to prevent re-detention. Your investment also enable us to adapt to our rapidly changing detention landscape. One of the most significant shifts has been transforming NYIFUP from a purely court-based model into a hybrid system that includes both [inaudible]

street intake and community-based referrals. Since launching our public referral form in August of last year, we have received more than a thousand direct referrals from families, teachers, hospitals, social workers and community organizations to name a few. Because ICE now transfers New Yorkers all over the country, our work must follow them. At any moment we are representing people held in facilities across roughly 15 states. Your support ensures that our clients are not abandoned simply because they are removed far from home. We have also expanded our impacts with partnerships. Our Habeas pro bono project has trained attorneys from eight major law firms, resulting in more than 20 petitions filed so far. Every adjudicated case has been successful. We’ve also provided technical assistance to advocate across the city who are engaging in detained work for the first time. We are deeply grateful for your support. It has allowed us not only to respond to crisis, but to be a lot stronger, more resilient system for immigrant New Yorkers. I’ll now turn it over to my colleague who will speak about how we plan to continue expanding our reach so that no New Yorker ever has to face deportation alone. Thank you.

My name is Deborah Lee and I’m the attorney in charge of the Immigration Law Unit at the Legal Aid Society. Thank you, Chair Encarnacion, for this opportunity and this committee for its continued support and partnership. The immigration landscape today, as we have heard, is more chaotic and demanding than at any point in recent memory. Since January 2025, our teams have had to track more than 600 immigration policy actions and over 50 new precedent decisions, each narrowing relief and increasing the complexity of every case we handle. Inside the courts, instability is escalating. Immigration judges are being reassigned at unprecedented rates, leading to inconsistent and hostile adjudication. Hearings are being cancelled with little notice and our clients are at constant risk of ICE detention. All this means that defending immigrants today increasingly requires not only Immigration Court advocacy, but also urgent habeas litigation, petitions for review and Federal Court interventions. This moment requires decisive city support. As the Bronx Defenders and Brooklyn Defender Services have testified, NYIFUP providers are the experts in defending these New Yorkers, people at

imminent risk of being removed from the United States and are likely forever separated from their families. We are best positioned to protect these vulnerable New Yorkers. To meet the need, we respectfully request increased support from the City Council for NYIFUP in the amount of $13.299 million for each provider. Despite all this, we remain hopeful. We continue strengthening our partnerships with pro bono law firms, law schools, and each NYIFUP provider is offering a new class of law graduates this fall. All these partners are joining us because they understand what is at stake for New Yorkers. Separately, LAS, Legal Aid, is respectfully requesting $4.5 million for the unaccompanied minors and families initiative, $1.75 million for the Protecting New Yorkers Habeas Initiative, and $580,596 to sustain our low-wage worker initiative. With the Council’s partnership we can protect New Yorkers and defend due process. Thank you.
Thank you. And I just wanted to ask you really quickly, you said $13.299 million for each of the providers, and that’s an increase from what?
Last year’s award was $8.299, [inaudible] per organization.
Per organization, alright, thank you.
Thank you very much.

Okay. Good afternoon, Chair Encarnacion and members of the Immigration Committee. My name is Tania Mattos and I am the Executive Director of Unlocal, an immigration nonprofit dedicated to serving New York’s immigrant communities through immigration legal services and

community education. Our team of lawyers, advocates, organizers, and social workers provide free services to immigrants across the five boroughs, including Know Your Rights and deportation defense workshops, New York City Dream Act application support, and workforce development support, as well as direct legal representation. Through programs including our Pro Se Plus project that is housed under the ASLAN network, the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative, and Queer Immigrant Justice Project and our general practice, we take a holistic and [inaudible] detention approach to the immigration legal services work that we do. We not only represent clients in proceedings, we equip communities with the tools and emergency preparedness and resources they need to respond safely and effectively when federal immigration enforcements comes to their door. As ICE actively intensifies in our streets and our airports, the demand for these services has not been greater. I’m going to skip forward. Beyond legal representation, the RLC trains legal practitioners on cutting edge immigration strategies, strengthens the entire legal services field and also provides rapid response social work services, offering direct

support and counseling to individuals facing deportations and the families they leave behind. What I urge the Council to provide is maintain funding for the rapid response legal collaborative services and commit to multi-year stable funding so providers can plan and serve clients reliably. And I’d like to share a very quick story of a father of– family of four who unfortunately father was– his limbs were lost in an accident, but we were able to provide rapid response legal services so they can focus on the emergency care that they needed and not focus on their removal orders, and that’s just one quick story I wanted to share.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Encarnacion, Council Members and staff. My name is Allison Cutler and I’m a supervising attorney in the Immigrant Protection Unit at the New York Legal Assistance Group. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the Preliminary Budget for fiscal year 2027. I supervise the Pro Se Plus project which has evolved from pro se application assistance to in-court advocacy for families facing the harshest aspects of immigration enforcement. My team is

regularly at 26 Federal Plaza helping individuals who are there for routine check-ins and court hearings, providing safety planning, appearing in front of court, intervening when appropriate while individuals are being wrongly detained, notifying families, and connecting them to vital post-detention support. NYLAG is grateful for the city and Council’s continued commitment to New York City’s immigrant communities. Today, we find ourselves in a terrifying moment. Our immigrant neighbors are being torn from their homes, families, and lives. Longstanding pathways to relief have ended, and enforcement is intensifying. These rapid changes underscore the need for increased flexible multi-year funding that allows providers to be innovative in our response. New York City legal service providers have a long history of meeting the moment with innovation, working with the city to create programs like ICARE, the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative, and Pro Se Plus project. Today, I’m testifying to ask the city to double-down on your commitment to our immigrant communities through expanded and flexible funding for immigration legal services. This includes sustained and increased funding for ASLAN and the Pro Se Plus

project, the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative which supports detained immigrants who do not qualify for NYFIUP, and also the legal support center model which has impacted our ability to continue to maintain services in partnerships with hospitals and other culturally-specific CBOs and we are grateful that we currently have one year LSE funding to continue providing services. We are so appreciative for your support, partnership and advocacy. Thank you.
